Question: Is it bad to use built-in language features in technical interviews??
Answer: In an interview, half of it is about the chemistry between you and the interviewer. When you do what you just said, then an interviewer could feel a mix of the following: 1. You are making fun of the interview question and hence indirectly you are making fun of me and the company I work at. 2. You are arrogant/childish. You probably already knew what you were supposed to do, but you are still not doing it. 3. You are not a very curious person. You didn't have the curiosity to learn how something as basic like that works, or even to read about how interviewing works. Now, if you get a seasoned interviewer, they will get past these feelings and politely nudge you to implement the algorithm (e.g. "You are right! Could you tell me how reverse works? Have you looked it up before? Yes? Great; please explain. No? That's okay! Let's try to implement it now!"). If you don't get a seasoned interviewer, then it won't matter if you are right or wrong. They will have mentally already rejected you. At least, your score would fall in their eyes. Deeper question you may be asking, is why do they expect you to dive deeper with such questions? A few reasons for that: 1. An urge to dive beyond the surface level is a strong indicator of your interest in the career you have chosen to pursue. The less black-boxes you mentally have, the better you are likely to succeed in that area. 2. If they simply wanted someone who could cobble functions and APIs together, they'd hire a pair of hands to do C++ for cheap (there are many avenues to do that). They don't what that. They want a mind to come with that pair of hands. A mind that is excited to dig deeper to get a better understanding of things. 3. If it's a company worth working for, then they are simply getting a lot of qualified applicants for the same position. They hence have to find some way to filter candidates out. If you stop at writing in-built functions, you can, but I bet that they'll get someone else who will not question their judgement, write what was expected of them, and get that job.

Question: Is there a developer shortage?
Answer: [Image from, @ Kelukelugames on Twitter] Many companies claim that there is a shortage of smart developers, who have experience in X. I beg to differ. There isn’t a shortage of smart developers. Most companies do not know what level of smartness they need for the kind of work they do and more importantly, how to test for it. e.g., Writing an API call doesn’t require the same level of smarts as rotating a binary tree. There isn’t a shortage of experienced developers either. Most companies are too impatient to give them experience with the skills they need. Then they spend the same amount of time looking for talent, in which they could have given a very useful headstart to someone. There isn’t a shortage of developers, period. Most companies choose to ignore everyone who applies to them, spending hundreds of thousands of $ on outbound cold-emailing and cold-calling in search of some mythical “ninja” developers. Question: How can I be a better programmer? I’m starting college and we need to learn Java. I’m feeling like I’m not good at all. I read the book, watch videos, and practice on CodeAcademy, but I’m not sure what else to do.
Answer: Thomas Alva Edison once said: “None of my inventions came by accident. I see a worthwhile need to be met and I make trial after trial until it comes. What it boils down to is one per cent inspiration and ninety-nine per cent perspiration.” Yes, you’re not inventing stuff at the pace Edison was. But from where you are, this is nothing short of an invention. Something totally new. Your perspiration looks correct, but if you feel that you’re still not succeeding, then one of the following is happening: If I were to teach you, I’d say you should start with a real need first. Something tangible, something that you can use in real life for someone e.g. your neighbor’s website, your barber’s app, or even your little sibling’s calculator. Something that is real and programmable in Java. As you go thru that project, you’ll have challenges to overcome. If you are interested in problem-solving (which is important to build a career in this field), you’ll naturally continue to address those challenges. You’ll learn, you’ll find people and resources that will help you and sooner or later, you’ll finish the job. All with Java, because that’s how you chose to do it. You may not write idiomatic Java, or the most perfect JavaDoc-strict Java, or with the most awesome design, but you will have solved a problem for someone. (which is what a programming language is ultimately supposed to do). It will take time, and it will take longer than what you think, but it’ll be worthwhile. Ideally you’d take this path under someone’s guidance, but it’s doable even without. If you’re not able to find a mentor, or you’re not able to overcome obstacles on your own, then that’s a strong indication that your heart is not in this (reason#1 above). But once you’re able to do this, it will inspire you. It will give you the right perspective to learn. It will help you shorten your learning curve, because you now know what is more important to learn. As you go down this path, you’ll start to see and use the power of Java to do more complex systems. The language, it’s ceremony, it’s efficiency and idiosyncrasies will pull you in more and more. More importantly, your successes with the language will feed your passion and you’ll never look back. God speed.

Question: A Google guy said that he can get me a Google software engineer job without going through the technical interview, should I trust him?
Answer: He very likely means, that he can get you a job there as a contractor, with a light weight technical interview process. Some (increasingly fewer) contracting roles at Google have a short technical interview process (and often not algorithms). Almost all those roles are highly specific to the skill set required. Those roles usually go through a contracting vendor, who has a previously trusted relationship with the hiring manager. So if your background is a great match for what the hiring manager is looking for, and the vendor you go thru has a trusted relationship with them (e.g. Because the vendor found some very good people previously for that manager), then there is a good chance that your interview process will be short. But in no case the technical interview will be eliminated for any software engineering position at Google. Certainly not for full time roles. Even if you know Larry Page (Larry, of all people, is known to be more ethically strict). Don't even try it.
